title: epan: Widen input value in relative time_[m]secs_to_str functions
description:
The internal implementations of [un]signed_time_secs_to_str_buf all
handle 64-bit value correctly, so there's no need to artificially limit
the inputs of the exported functions to 32-bits. While a value that does
not fit in 32-bits is unlikely for the seconds variants, it's not entirely
unreasonable to have a relative time value that doesn't fit in a 32-bit
integer when expressed in milliseconds. (I.e., 25 days or more signed,
50 days or more unsigned.) It is unlikely to need any value that doesn't
fit in a 64-bit signed integer, so the only function that takes
milliseconds taking a signed value should work; both signed and unsigned
32-bit intgers will convert to 64-bit signed integers without loss.

All the actually existing uses of signed_time_msecs_to_str seem to take
what is retrieved as an unsigned 32-bit integer and pass it into the
function. In practice, since these values are unlikely to be that large
in truth (many of them are "milliseconds since midnight, for example),
the result didn't matter, but with hypothetical large values they would
have produced the wrong value.

It is possible that some dissector would have retrieved and stored a
signed time value in an unsigned integer, and then passed it into one
of these functions, depending on the exact semantics of unsigned to
signed 32-bit integer conversion. If so, that was a bug in the
dissector. It does not appear to be the case in any dissector in the
main repository.

In one case (packet-smb-pipe.c) an unsigned value was cast to signed
before passing in this function, but this was incorrect and only because
the use in the function predated the existence of the unsigned function.
(Compare the dates of 7221f30ab3266400b2c848fd39f10c6c9bc00a70 to
the commit e18fdae9b6525b6bfbf5256b08d970e8fcf286a2; the explicit cast
was later added to address warnings in 411249419dc399c8fcf5a364a90067f864626ba1)
That cast is removed. (The unsigned function need not be used because
the value is 32-bits.)
In another case (packet-dhcp.c) an explicit case of unsigned to signed
was intentional; the cast is necessary because of the parameters for
custom format function pointers (CF_FUNC).

It has long been the case in C (e.g., see C11 6.3.1.3) that converting
a signed integer to an unsigned is done "by repeatedly or subtracting
one more than the maximum value that can be represented in the new type
until the value is in the range of the new type."[1, 6.3.1.3] It has
equally long been specified that unsigned integer types "shall be capable
of representing values from 0 to 2^N − 1".[1, 6.2.6.2]

That means that the answer to the parenthetical comment has been true,
so it is removed.

[1] - https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

 }
 
 char *
-unsigned_time_secs_to_str(wmem_allocator_t *scope, const uint32_t time_val)
+unsigned_time_secs_to_str(wmem_allocator_t *scope, const uint64_t time_val)
 {
     wmem_strbuf_t *buf;
 
@@ -407,10 +407,6 @@ signed_time_secs_to_str_buf(int64_t time_val, const uint32_t frac,
              * a 64-bit signed integer.  Just directly
              * pass UINT64_MAX, which is its absolute
              * value, directly to unsigned_time_secs_to_str_buf().
-             *
-             * (XXX - does ISO C guarantee that -(-2^n),
-             * when calculated and cast to an n-bit unsigned
-             * integer type, will have the value 2^n?)
              */
             unsigned_time_secs_to_str_buf(UINT64_MAX, frac,
                 is_nsecs, buf);
@@ -427,7 +423,7 @@ signed_time_secs_to_str_buf(int64_t time_val, const uint32_t frac,
 }
 
 char *
-signed_time_secs_to_str(wmem_allocator_t *scope, const int32_t time_val)
+signed_time_secs_to_str(wmem_allocator_t *scope, const int64_t time_val)
 {
     wmem_strbuf_t *buf;
 
@@ -447,7 +443,7 @@ signed_time_secs_to_str(wmem_allocator_t *scope, const int32_t time_val)
  * hours, minutes, and seconds, and put the result into a buffer.
  */

 {

     int msecs;
